metaDescription: Bentleyville mineral owners: old coal-town split estates meet modern Marcellus leases. Get a clear offer explained in plain terms.
heroLead: Bentleyville was a coal patch town long before Marcellus, and a lot of the mineral ownership here still reflects that older split-estate history.
intro: For most of the twentieth century, Bentleyville's economy ran on coal, and a lot of family farms in the area sold off their coal rights to a mining company generations ago while holding onto the oil and gas underneath. That means a fair number of owners here actually hold a cleaner mineral interest than they realize, because the coal severance already separated out one layer of the estate long before shale gas ever became relevant.

We know how confusing it is to untangle who owns what when a deed references coal rights from the 1920s alongside gas rights from 2010. That's exactly the kind of title work we do before we ever hand you a number.

sections.heading: Coal legacy, gas present
paragraphs: If your family's Bentleyville-area deed shows a coal severance from decades back, that history doesn't affect your oil and gas rights unless the same deed specifically carved those out too. We check both layers when we review title, because it's a common source of confusion for owners who assume 'we sold the minerals' meant everything underground, when it usually meant just the coal seam.

This part of Washington County sits in the wet-gas Marcellus fairway, and operators here have been actively developing units for over a decade, so most producing tracts near Bentleyville have a real royalty history to evaluate.

sections.heading: What your royalty statement is really telling you
paragraphs: Between natural decline curves, gas price swings, and post-production cost deductions allowed under Pennsylvania law since Kilmer v. Elexco, a Bentleyville royalty check rarely looks the same two quarters in a row. We'll go through your actual statement with you and explain each line rather than leaving you to guess.

sections.heading: Selling without losing sleep over it
paragraphs: A mineral sale doesn't touch your surface property or your home; it's limited to the subsurface rights and the royalty they generate. For owners tired of watching an unpredictable check shrink, converting that future income into a lump sum now removes the guesswork entirely.

faqs.question: My deed mentions coal rights sold separately. Does that affect my gas rights?
faqs.answer: Not unless the same deed specifically severed the oil and gas too. We'll trace exactly what was sold and what your family retained.

faqs.question: Will selling affect my house or land above ground?
faqs.answer: No. A mineral sale is limited to subsurface oil and gas rights; your surface property is unaffected.

faqs.question: How do you value a coal-town legacy interest like this?
faqs.answer: We look at your confirmed net mineral acreage, current lease terms, unit production, and recent royalty history, the same process regardless of how the title developed historically.
